Zoning By-law, tax amendments for garden and garage suites and secondary suites. If I could get a mover for first reading of By-law Number 10179, moved by Councillor Donauer or seconded by Councillor MacDonald? Is anyone opposed? That carries. And the hearing is now open, and I will turn it over to our administration.

Thank you, Madam Chair. My name is Paul Katosik Toes. I am a senior planner in the Planning and Development Department. Tonight, I will be presenting the Zoning By-law tax amendments affecting garden and garage suite regulations, and for six-unit, multiple-unit dwellings on corner sites in the transit development area. The amendments that you are considering tonight have been separated into two public hearings, one for each matter. The project background will be provided in the first presentation. By-law Number 10179 provides the amendments for garden and garage suites. Next slide, please.

This slide provides background. Under the Housing Action Plan and our agreement to receive funding under the Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF), the City committed to reviewing the regulations for infill development. In regard to the HAF targets, while we have met some of them, housing is still needed in our community, and the amendments are intended to provide opportunities for additional housing units. We retain to consult and middle and small housing to complete a report. We received it at the end of 2020-25, and it provided recommendations for changes to the garden and garage suite regulations for primary dwellings, which are one- and two-unit dwellings and four-unit dwellings in the established neighborhoods, and multiple-unit dwellings on corner sites. This is the first of two reports recommending Zoning amendments, and the next report will be on amendments to primary dwellings, and we anticipate that will come to Council in July. Next slide, please.

So, infill development generally occurs within the established neighborhoods. The established neighborhoods map is an appendix to the Zoning By-law, and this includes those within Circle Drive, plus Montgomery Place, Forest Grove, and Southern Wind. The map includes two categories of neighborhoods: the blue area for the pre-World War II neighborhoods, and the pink for the post-war, and this is a general classification. As background, these categories were developed with the neighborhood-level infill development strategy that was done in 2013. The regulations that exist today for garden and garage suites and primary dwellings were developed from the recommendations provided from this strategy. There are specific regulations currently applied for each category for primary dwellings and garden and garage suites. Next slide, please.

Garden and garage suites are detached dwelling units on the same site as a one-unit, two-unit, or semi-detached dwelling. A garden suite is a suite located at grade, and a garage suite, like the one shown on the screen, contains a dwelling unit and a garage space in the same building. I'd just like to note that the pictures throughout this presentation are of existing garden and garage suites in Saskatoon that are already built. The regulations for garden and garage suites have been in place for ten-plus years, and over time they've become an accepted form of development in our city. The proposed amendments to garden and garage suites are to allow for a two-story structure on appropriate sites within the established neighborhood. Next slide, please.

The proposed amendments are as follows: Currently, one garden garage suite is allowed accessory to a two-unit dwelling, and it is proposed to allow two suites in addition to the two-unit dwelling on a site with a minimum lot width of 15 meters. We're proposing to remove the neighborhood categories which restricted the development of the suite to one story and to allow for two-story on sites with access to a rear lane. The sites that the two-story structures are proposed to be allowed are suitable for development in the Category 2 neighborhoods. As they are required to have a lane, the sites are often very wide at 15 meters and have lengths ranging from 100 feet to 150 feet. The following details of the amendments are in addition to the information in the attached report to MPC.

We're maintaining the mass regulations. The regulations are consistent with the existing regulations for a garage suite, and for a garden suite of one story, the height is consistent with a detached garage that's currently permitted. The sidewalk height requirement was eliminated because it was redundant due to a previous amendment that removed building setbacks for the second story. The overall height of the suite is regulated, and the By-law requires that the second story be up to 80% of the area of the main floor, which is intended to break up the massing. The clarifying development standards include: As the current regulations did not allow for a path to the flanking street on a corner site and provided for the path from the front to the rear lane, the proposed amendment has been amended to accommodate this access, and the wording has changed to provide a path of 0.75 meters and is hard surface. Although this regulation may not strictly meet barrier-free requirements, these are internal pathways on private properties and not necessarily pathways that will be used by the tenant. The path could be built as wide as necessary for any additional tenant that's occupying either the one-unit dwelling or the garden or garage suite.

Another change that is proposed: we are allowing for a balcony on all sides, and it will no longer be restricted to face the lane or the flanking street. This will be permitted provided that screening with non-transparent materials is provided. So, this slide shows all three categories that apply to garden or garage suites: the blue ones, Category 1; the pink ones, Category 2; and the green ones that are Category 3 or greenfield neighborhoods. The amendments in front of you tonight will remove this map and allow for a two-story structure on all sites with a rear lane and one story for all other sites. This picture is of a development by North Prairie Development in Rosewood that contains suites facing the rear lane on a greenfield site. Next slide, please.

As previously mentioned, it is proposed for garden suites to allow for two suites, accessory to a two-unit dwelling, which is shown on the green picture. Four units per site are permitted in the other forms on a 15-meter wide site, and on the screen you see a semi-detached unit with two garden or garage suites, two detached one-unit dwellings with garage suites, as well as a four-unit dwelling. Next slide, please.

So, this slide compares the heights of buildings permitted in low-density neighborhoods. On the far left, we have an example of a bungalow that is very common across the city, particularly in the older neighborhoods. The height of this bungalow is approximately 3.7 meters to the midpoint. Next is a detached garage. So, you see the maximum height is 5 meters to the top of the peak. This will be the maximum height for any one-story garden or garage suite developed on a site without a lane. The next one is the two-story garage suite; the maximum height of this structure is 6.5 meters to the midpoint of the peak. The overall height, in particular on the example shown today, really depends on the pitch of the roof, but it gives an accurate description. And then lastly, the height of a two-story dwelling, a maximum height of 8.5 meters to the peak, and this is permitted across the established neighborhoods. Next slide, please.

This slide provides the engagement that was undertaken for these amendments. This engagement indicated that people were supportive of the change by allowing a two-story structure in the remainder of the established neighborhood. Some concerns were expressed, including the number of suites on the site, parking on local streets, and servicing capacity. We also received a number of inquiries from people wanting to build this form of structure on their lot in a neighborhood where only one story is permitted. We note that letters of support have been received from Rental Housing Saskatchewan and the Saskatchewan Realtors Association. The amendments were received, were reviewed by the applicable city departments, and no comments were received that would preclude this from going forward. Prior to this being considered by City Council, the amendments were advertised in accordance with the public notice policy. And following our review, administration is recommending approval of the Zoning Bylaw text amendments. This concludes my presentation. Thank you. Thank you very much. We'll go now to Mr. Hurley and the Municipal Planning Commission. Thank you. The Municipal Planning Commission, at its regular meeting held on April 28th, 2026, considered the report of the Community Services Division regarding proposed Zoning Bylaw text amendments for garage and garden suites, and secondary suites. The commission's report, attached to the agenda, and my comments this evening will also stand for the proposed Zoning Bylaw text amendments for development on corner lots in the transit development area in item 5.1.7. During the meeting, administration responded to questions of the commission regarding height restrictions for garden and garage suites in relation to existing neighborhood development, and the rationale for proposing six units on corner lots in the transit development area as a discretionary use. Administration also noted that progressions from discretionary to permitted use have occurred with secondary suites and garden and garage suites gradually over time after careful consideration and review. No concerns were expressed by the commission, and we are recommending that the proposed Zoning Bylaw text amendments for garage and garden and garage suites, secondary suites, and for the development on corner lots in the transit development area be approved. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Hurley. Other questions for Mr. Hurley? I'm not seeing any, but thank you very much. We're going to move to public presentations, welcoming the South Canadian Regional Builders Association. Hello. Good evening, Your Worship and members of Council, and thank you for the opportunity to speak tonight. My name is Michael Berges. I'm here representing the South Canadian Regional Builders Association to speak in support of the first package of Zoning Bylaw amendments coming out of the city's infill review process. I want to acknowledge the work that went into this by administration to get to these recommendations. While the recommendations might seem very practical and quite modest, I recognize that the work to get here is neither easy nor simple. Infill regulations are complex, not only because of the technical considerations, but because they also require balancing public expectations, servicing questions, financial considerations, as well as the consideration of many different perspectives of how our city should grow and where. From our perspective, the package reflects a careful review of specific barriers that have been limiting practical infill opportunities in our city. These are not sweeping changes; these are targeted, measured amendments that improve consistency, reduce unnecessary friction, and help create opportunities for housing where the site conditions make sense. The reality is that Saskatoon has strong policy goals for infill, but our rule book hasn't always kept pace with those goals. That's not simply an industry opinion. The independent consultants engaged through the city's review identified very specific barriers in our current regulations: barriers that affect design (and not in a good way), feasibility, consistency, and ultimately whether infill projects could go forward or not. In other words, the challenge is not whether Saskatoon supports infill; in principle, on paper, we do. The real question is whether our regulations allow it to happen in practice. As Council is aware, Saskatoon has set ambitious targets for infill growth, but the hard truth is we are nowhere close to meeting them. According to the city's most recent growth monitoring report, only 9.5% of residential development occurred through infill the previous year, the lowest in more than a decade, and the five-year rolling average is sitting at only 11.6%. I think we can do better than that. So while we have strong policy direction on paper, the results tell us something very important: the gap is not closing on its own. If Saskatoon truly wants more infill housing, and I think we do, we cannot keep just reaffirming the goal. We have to actually start to remove barriers that are preventing practical, modest infill from being built. The good news is the city has recognized the same thing: policy direction alone is not enough. That is why the Housing Action Plan identified accessory-dwelling units and infill development as key priorities, and that is why Council directed administration to commission a comprehensive review to identify what was standing in the way. What is before Council tonight starts to respond directly to those findings. Now, I want to be clear about something: these amendments will not solve Saskatoon's housing challenge on their own, but they do matter, because no single zoning amendment builds a home, but every single unnecessary barrier can stop one from being built. Now, to put it simply, these amendments really do three practical things: they create clarity, consistency, and provide more opportunities for the kind of housing Saskatoon needs, including more options for renters, aging parents, adult children, and homeowners looking to offset rising costs. But most importantly, this is a balanced approach: it removes unnecessary barriers while still maintaining appropriate rules and oversight. And I think it's important to be clear: these amendments are not a radical departure from what Saskatoon already allows. For example, two-story garden and garage suites are already permitted, as you saw, in Category 1 and Category 3 neighborhoods. This amendment simply extends the same opportunity to Category 2, where back lane access exists and the same standards can be met. In other words, if the site conditions are the same, the rules should be the same. That is not a big leap; that's just consistency. At the end of the day, Council has decided that infill should be a part of Saskatoon's growth. The growth monitoring report tells us we are not there yet, and while these amendments alone will not close that gap, they are a practical and overdue step in the right direction. Needless to say, we strongly support these amendments and hope that Council supports them too. Thank you. We'll go on to a question from Councillor Donauer. Thank you, Worship. Thank you for the presentation tonight, Ms. Berges. You made reference to barriers to infill and that we're not meeting our targets. You talked about how this will be a partial solve, not everything. I know this is a big question that could have a very complex answer, but what does your organization see as the next few big barriers that need to be addressed in the city so that we can make some progress on this? Absolutely. This is reiterated and confirmed, I guess, in the report and all the work that has been done. This has been a year in the making, really, to get here, so it's important work that's done. The things that I hear most often from infill builders are really the challenges around sidewalk setbacks and percent site coverage, right? Those are the second one: percent site coverage. Thank you. Those are the ones that come up time and time again, as well as setbacks and those sorts of things. The other barrier is also consistency and certainty, really understanding what is allowed with any given site. When you have inconsistent rules based on arbitrary things like neighborhood category, it makes it quite challenging. Okay, thank you very much. Thank you. I don't see any other questions, but thank you very much for joining us. And now I believe we're going online. Sherry Terrace Off, can you hear me? Yes, I can. Can you hear me? Yes, we can. You can begin when you're ready. Thank you, Your Worship and Council, for this opportunity to speak this evening. My name is Sherry Terrace Off. I have submitted a short video that I would like to be played first, and then I have some comments afterwards. Proposed changes to Garden and Garage Suites. I do not support this proposed zoning amendment for many reasons. Massing. By consolidating the tables for readability, the sidewalk height maximum standard has been eliminated. Both the engaged page and the project update email indicated that in addition to height and setback, massing controls would remain in place. What are those controls now? How are affected homeowners and communities protected? Accessibility. I compared the current zoning by-law to the proposed one. While the current by-law contemplates an internal path, the width of which should accommodate barrier-free access, the proposed by-law considers an internal hard-surface path with a minimum width of 0.75 meters. How does 2.4 feet allow for wheelchair access? Targets. The half initiative for accessory dwellings has a target of an estimated 30 units. Through a permit search online, 60 permits for garden and garage suites have been submitted since the last amendments were approved in April 2024 to reduce barriers for building accessory dwelling units. Category 1 had 20 permits. Category 2 had five. Category 3 had 35 permits. Specifically, Rosewood had 29 of them on two blocks. This is what they look like. On their marketing website, the one-bedroom units are 564 square feet and will be rented for just under $1,700 a month. This is just a sampling of the neighborhoods and wards that could expect to see this in their backyards: Mayfair, Montgomery, Fairhaven, Dundonald, Silverwood Heights, Holliston, Avalon, College Park, Lakeview, and Erindale. Missing middle targets. According to the latest progress on housing supply targets document, the housing target for the missing middle category was exceeded in 2024 alone. Clearly, this proposed amendment is not required to increase the housing supply for missing middle. In conclusion, while this amendment reduces barriers to development, it further removes homeowner rights for existing neighborhoods. And it still does not provide the standard required for accessibility. Thank you. And just to follow up with that, can you hear me? Yes, you can. Okay. When the information about the proposed zoning amendments was sent to community associations, I assume each neighborhood across the city got the same thing: a document with a lot of text and perhaps a map. This is a difficult format to understand zoning changes. A graphic would be more effective. Even the consultant's report had a visualization of the current differences between Categories 1 and 3, and Category 2. As Category 2 neighborhoods will be most impacted by this amendment, Category 2 community associations specifically would have benefited from images that highlight the changes, as by-law jargon is confusing. And in its presentation tonight, they showed examples of height differences. I would also be interested in what a two-story garage suite would look like with the balconies on the side. What this by-law amendment does is address the physical attributes of garden and garage suites. What this by-law amendment does not do is dictate how they function. They could be affordable units, or they could be overpriced units. They could be rental homes to increase the housing supply, or they could be Airbnbs for short-term accommodations. The zoning amendment on its own does not directly dictate the affordability of new development. Nor does it necessarily increase the supply of home rental units. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Terrace Off. Do we have questions of this speaker? I'm not seeing any, but thank you again, and thank you for your video. I want to ask if anyone else in the gallery would like to return. Is anyone now exiting? I'm not seeing anyone else that wants to speak to this item. So we'll go now to questions of our administration. Councillor Dubois. Thank you, Mayor Block, through you to the administration. So it was mentioned by the last speaker, but I have made a note of that. Can you tell me why the massing has been eliminated through this proposal? Thank you for the question. Through the Chair, massing has not been eliminated. There are several regulations that regulate the massing of a garden and garage suite, including the wall length, the area that it can provide, the maximum height, and the setback, or the 80% requirement for the second floor. The massing requirements have not been removed. The only one we removed was a four-meter side wall height, which was redundant. So, just to provide a little bit of background: back in 2014, when we were developing the regulations for garden and garage suites, the form at that time looked like a cake. So you had your garage, and then there was to be a step back on either side to put the garden and garage suite. This proved to be very expensive and more difficult for the builders to build. So we amended the regulations to allow for it to be 80% of the size of the second floor, and that 20% is typically a balcony. So we have not eliminated any massing requirements. I appreciate that. Ms. Burgess did mention that that was a barrier. So, in the engagement with the home builders, was that a discussion between you folks? Not removal of that specifically. What we really talked about was that this form of development is restricted in the Category 2 neighborhoods, such as Adelaide Churchill, Mayfair, Forest Grove, and several others, on sites that were large and appropriate. I guess larger than in some areas of the city and have lanes. Those are older areas of the city. I live in that neighborhood. My house was built in 1960. I have a large lot. So in those neighborhoods, the two-story form is appropriate. Other than that, one story is permitted. So now two stories are permitted city-wide on sites with lanes, if Council approves this, sorry. But when I asked you if administration had discussed this, because Ms. Burgess did mention that the sidewalk through this process was a barrier. Sorry, through the Chair, that's in regard to primary dwellings, the sidewalk. Well, that's actually a different thing. It's not in regard to garden and garage suites. Okay, so could you talk to me about that sidewalk then? Sure. So there's a regulation that applies to primary dwellings, one-unit and detached, that restricts the size of the dwelling based on the area of the sidewalk, the sidewalk that faces the neighbors. It's based on a formula depending on how wide your lot is and what your setbacks are. So that really restricts the size of your primary dwelling or your one-unit dwelling. Myself and my colleagues are working with Ms. Burgess and several developers in the city on amendments to that regulation. And that's what's coming forward in July. Okay, so if this was approved today, then you would be bringing forward in July an amendment to what? Regardless of what is approved today. Okay, regardless of what happens today, we'll still be bringing that forward in July. Okay, very good. Thank you. And then the accessibility that was mentioned, with that minimum width of 0.75 meters and not enough space for a wheelchair, can you talk to me about that, please? The wording of the former regulations said it "should accommodate barrier-free access," but we put in a requirement that it be a minimum of 0.75 and be a hard surface. I just want to reiterate to Council, these are internal paths. This is like your path from your house to your garage on your site. So if you're building your garage suite to accommodate someone in a wheelchair, you can build it as wide as you want; there's nothing that precludes you from doing that. These are internal pathways that this regulation applies to. So if someone is living in one of these suites that has accessibility issues, then the sidewalk could be built to accommodate whatever kind of mobility device they have.
Through the Chair, that's correct. And so, is it correct that prior to you bringing this forward today, when we had garage suites or these garden suites, it was a discretionary use? But with this today, it would be a blanket approval so that you don't have to come to us each time that there's an application for one of these suites. Is that correct?
Through the Chair, not quite. They were discretionary when they were first approved in 2014. In 2022, or 2021, under the zoning bylaw review, garden and garage suites went from discretionary to permitted. So they're now permitted citywide. They're permitted citywide already. And what this change will do is allow for the two-story structure on Category 2 neighborhoods. Thank you. I thought we had to approve that prior.
The other thing that Ms. Burgess mentioned was the percentage by coverage. It was also barrier. Through the Chair, that also applies to primary dwellings, not garden and garage suites. Thank you very much. I'm going to answer the question. Thank you. Your Worship, through you to administration, I'm just curious, I know other municipalities are looking at infill development in these types of programs. How are we compared to what you're proposing now, and how are those types of programs progressing in other municipalities?
Through the Chair, thank you for the question. The report included a municipal scan; I believe it was Attachment One to the report. Generally, garden and garage suites, or laneway suites, are permitted in most major cities across Saskatchewan and Canada. Through our research, we found that there are many different standards and approaches, and each city does it a little bit differently. But how has the response been in the communities?
In some cities, such as Calgary and Edmonton, there has been a bigger uptake for a number of reasons. Within Saskatchewan cities, there are Saskatchewan cities where there has been some uptake. I think this is probably a good time to mention that building a garage suite or garden suite is like building a second house on your site. And certainly, in an infill situation, the services are in the front street. So you either have to connect your services to the front street or through the house through some complicated plumbing that I don't understand. But there has been an uptake; I believe we have about 55 to 60 citywide currently.
In the report, it mentions that this also supports half funding. I'm just curious, I thought that was all allocated, and how does this program, how does our decision on this impact our half funding?
Through the Chair, it doesn't impact it. But one of the conditions of our half funding was that we approve, or rather, that we review the infill regulations. That was one of the conditions of the report. So CMHC is eagerly waiting for the outcome of these public hearings to get word that we have met that condition. And if we didn't meet that condition, what happens? The City of Saskatoon would be under further scrutiny from CMHC. I'm just looking at my colleague, Ms. Gutman; I don't know if she has anything else to add.
Christine Gutman, Senior Project Planner with Planning and Development: Yes, this was one of our initiatives under the CMHC Housing Accelerator Fund funding when we put together our housing action plan back in 2023. This was one of the initiatives that the city put forward as part of our housing action plan. It is one of our milestones within that to review our guidelines, our infill guidelines, and our infill regulations. They have told us that as we bring this forward, they are looking for us, of course, to approve them. If Council chooses not to or requests that we go back and look at something else, they would be looking at that as part of our annual review, which occurs at the end of the year. Good, thank you.
What protections still remain in place for privacy, massing, and neighborhood compatibility after these amendments? Thank you for the question, through the Chair. In regard to privacy and massing, the balconies are required to have solid screening and walls. Typically, I understand the question. In regard to privacy within any neighborhood, you do have an impact even with an existing dwelling. You have an impact on your neighbors in regard to privacy. I guess when a garden and garage suite is built, it is a change, and there is that activity directed towards the lane. Other than the balcony, we don't necessarily have any other protections. Most of them, the entrance door faces the rear lane. There's parking within the existing garden or garage suite.
Okay, and I just want to clarify, a property can actually have a garden suite or a garage suite, but one property couldn't have both a garden and a garage suite. They couldn't have up to three dwelling units. So the primary dwelling can have a secondary suite, like a basement suite, and there can be one in the rear yard. And that's an existing regulation that's already in place. Right, okay. And so the main criteria then is that there's a back alley for the two-story dwelling? I think those are my questions. Thank you.
Councillor: Thank you, Your Worship. I'm just trying to picture this. I mean, you mentioned that you live in a very established neighborhood. What thought is being given to these neighborhoods that are already established regarding servicing, if all of a sudden we get a huge influx of garden or garage suites?
Through the Chair, when we did the garden and garage suite review and the subsequent review under the zoning bylaw, we did work with our engineering colleagues. And there is capacity within the existing neighborhoods to accommodate secondary suites and garden and garage suites. So every single property had one. I'm just thinking of that map that showed there was a whole bunch of them right on one crescent. That's in a greenfield area. With greenfield, the servicing is new, and there is capacity in those areas for that number of dwelling units because it's built into the development plan. Okay, fair enough. Thank you.
Anderson, Director of Planning and Development: As Ms. Katasik Toath mentioned, when we brought forward all the amendments in 2024, there was extensive review with our colleagues in engineering to assess how we are going to deal with this across the city. Through the work we've been doing on the growth plan, we've been focused a lot on our corridors. And so we have a range of servicing assessments that have been done for those areas to ensure that we can do the development and do the developments that the city has been working towards in those areas. We know the assessment has been done there. Our colleagues in infrastructure are also very diligent in looking at how the servicing is working. What are the capacity needs, what are the development pressures that are coming, what are the trends we're seeing? So they do that all the time, and then we've embedded processes into reviews to ensure that there's an early check-in on whether there is capacity in a given area for any of these developments. In some cases, for example, when we have a larger scale of rezoning or something like that, it may be something that hadn't currently been considered there, and we go through a review process to ensure it can be dealt with. Sometimes that results in costs to the proponent to build in the additional capacity that's needed, but overall across the city, we don't expect to see what has been seen in that rose, for example, because that was planned for that work to happen. So we may see much more of that in our greenfield neighborhoods because that's something that can be built in from the beginning, planned for from the beginning. Neighbors can buy into that knowing that's what is around them. So we expect to see a bit more of it coming there. The ability and the speed and economics of doing that on every infill lot is just not there to see that in every case. So we don't expect to see that kind of pressure across the city at least for many, many years.

I'm just asking because it seems like if we're planning this clearly, there could be limitations on our infrastructure. Would that be reasonable to say? There absolutely could be limitations on the infrastructure, but as they said, our colleagues are very diligent in doing that work every day to ensure that upgrades are brought forward for funding and are identified and planned ahead of time so that we don't run into that situation.

So is the surface capacity determined with each permit, or is it also looked at holistically for the area as well? Both. It is both. So they do city-wide consistently, and then there are particular areas that they might focus on for any given reason. Stormwater flooding has been one of the things that they focused in particular areas, but then we have a review process where every permit can be assessed.

I won't go into parking and traffic concerns; I've just heard a lot of them. All right, thank you. I would have one further question for you, Ms. That's a cove. So thank you for the detailed information that you provided. It's a lot. I know we've been doing this for a lot of years, and just when I think I really understand it, I even answered some questions tonight that I feel like I just want to be sure how we're voting. I heard you say that you can have up to three on any site now, and you're recommending this in this new area that we haven't done before. So, I can't remember which appendix I'm looking at right now, but what it says there shall not be more than one garden suite or garage suite per site. They meant to permit two garden or garage suites. Accessory to a two-unit dwelling would be four units.

Through the chair to you, yes, that's correct. Okay, so can you just clarify one more time so that we're really clear about how we're voting? If I could just get the clerk to go to slide seven in my slide deck. So these all depict a 50-foot wide site, or 15 meters. So on the site, the top right one, you have a one-unit dwelling and you have a garage suite. You have a garage suite on either subdivided lot, and you can have a secondary suite in each of those. So it's three units on one strip, or three units on the next strip. With a semi-detached dwelling, it's the same thing if you move over to the left. So what we're saying for a two-unit dwelling, you have two units in your primary dwelling. The site has them unsubdivided, and you can have two garage suites in the back for a total of four units on the site.

Okay, that was different than how you answered it previously to another Councillor. At least that's a bit more clear now. Okay, and is that applicable city-wide, or is this just for this particular area? Through the Mayor, it's city-wide. Can you speak a little bit more to the category of neighborhood that we are talking about? You mentioned certain areas of the city, and I've gone through my notes again and I'm just not seeing exactly the spaces that you're speaking of. So if I could get the clerk, please, to go back to slide six. So this is the map that shows the regulations for garden and garage suites. So the blue is Category One, older neighborhoods, and the green is the greenfield neighborhoods. In those two areas, you can have a two-story garage suite currently. On the pink neighborhoods, you're limited to one story. So we're proposing to remove the categorization altogether, and on a site with a rear lane, you would be allowed two stories. If your site doesn't have a rear lane, you would be permitted one story. Okay. I think those are my questions. Thank you.

And I don't see any of the lights on for questions. Can I get someone to move receiving the reports? Moved by Councillor Randy Donauer and seconded by Councillor Ferris. That carries the resolution to close the hearing. Moved by Councillor Bev Dubois and seconded by Councillor Scott Ford. This is an opportunity for Councillors to provide any comments. Can I get someone to move second reading of the bylaw? Moved by Councillor Kathryn MacDonald and seconded by Councillor Senos Timon. Is anyone opposed? That carries permission for third reading of the bylaw. Moved by Councillor Jasmin Parker and seconded by Councillor Scott Ford. Is anyone opposed? That carries, and third reading of the bylaw. Moved by Councillor Senos Timon and seconded by Councillor Kathryn MacDonald. Seeing none opposed? And that is carried. Thank you. 5.1.7 Zoning Bylaw Text Amendments.

I'm going to select a special community plan at 702 and 706 Victoria Avenue. I'll turn it over to our administration. Wait a second, I mean, first reading of the bylaw. Moved by Councillor Robert Pearce, seconded by Councillor Kathryn MacDonald. Good evening to you and members of City Council. Recent zoning changes that have occurred through the Housing Accelerator Fund increased development rights at this location. A request to exceed the newly established four-story limit requires careful consideration. Following a detailed policy review, administration finds that the proposal aligns with relevant policies in our Official Community Plan due to the location characteristics of the site, the form and scale of the building, and its fit within the area context. To summarize a few of those main points of alignment from our policy, and I've noted some of these points already: The site is located within our transit development area along a major collector street. It's adjacent to the western boundary of the Nutana Cora Grove area. Downtown, the Broadway commercial area, parks, and other amenities are nearby. Transit and active transportation infrastructure in the area includes the future bus rapid transit on Broadway Avenue, which is within walking distance to the nearest stations. Existing cycle tracks on Victoria Avenue and the Meewasin Trail are nearby. The proposed design includes pedestrian-oriented building frontage, with street access dwelling units on Victoria Avenue that engage with the public realm and enhance the overall quality of the streetscape. Finally, a significant consideration with this application is that there is an existing pattern of medium- to high-density residential development in this area. The proposal at six stories provides a compatible and appropriate gradation of density to the surrounding neighborhood. I noted already that there are neighboring sites that are already designated high-density residential, and through controls in the zoning agreement, this development will be lower in height than the maximum heights allowed on nearby sites. Low-density residential land use is also separated and buffered from the site. In January of 2026, notification was provided to 353 property owners in the area, as well as the Nutana Community Association, Broadway Business Improvement District, Mara Residence Management Board, and the Ward 6 Councillor. An engaged page was launched on the city's website at that time, and notice signs were placed around the perimeter of the site. A public information meeting was held January 27th of this year at Nutana Legion; approximately 20 members of the public attended that event. Comments and questions received from the public to date have related to clarification of the proposal and the process; concerns regarding local traffic conditions, use of the rear lane, and impact during construction; as well as comments regarding sustainable building features for new development. Administration has responded to all correspondence with follow-up information related to the specific comments and questions received, and has not received additional feedback. A technical review was conducted for the application in accordance with our standard review process. No infrastructure or transportation-related concerns were identified from that review. I'll just note two items from the administration's review that are notable. We requested a heritage impact statement from the applicant. The applicant detailed from their perspective how the design and construction of their building considered the adjacent Mar residents so that any potential negative impacts to this important heritage resource would be mitigated. An urban forestry team also reviewed to ensure appropriate consideration for the retention and protection of the mature trees located in the 11th Street Boulevard. So, to conclude, Mayor Block, the proposal aligns with relevant objectives and policies contained in our official community plan. The proposal has been reviewed by other civic departments, and no concerns were identified which would preclude the application from proceeding. Public notices have been provided in accordance with the established procedures, and therefore, administration is recommending that the official community plan amendment to redesignate 702 and 706 Victoria Avenue for medium-density residential to high-density residential be approved. Four units are currently permitted city-wide on sites with a width of 50 meters or 50 feet. On corner sites within the Transit Development Area, the infill regulations do not apply. Therefore, on corners, the four-unit dwelling can be 10 meters in height, and the side yard regulations would not apply. The proposed amendment in front of you tonight will allow for six units within the same building envelope. Allowing for up to six units on corner sites would be allowed through the discretionary use process, subject to approval by City Council. This review would ensure appropriate consideration of site-specific context and potential neighborhood impacts. Applications proposing more than four units would be considered by City Council and must be consistent with the city-wide approach beyond four units. I'm clarifying that this is a discretionary use that can be accommodated within a zoning district only after additional review to evaluate the proposed use in relation to applicable policies, regulations, technical considerations, and the surrounding context. Corner sites are suitable for this form of development as there is access from the front and flanking streets and the rear lanes. In the report, we have included a number of evaluation criteria for this discretionary use: availability of on-street parking on both front and flanking streets, rear lane access, and an analysis demonstrating an acceptable parking plan.
